title: MITRE ATT&CK Concept Map
subtitle: The shared language for what attackers do, and the objects linked around each technique. Tap a bubble.
rootDesc: A free knowledge base, maintained by the non-profit MITRE, of adversary tactics and techniques observed in real attacks. It gives defenders, vendors, and threat reports one vocabulary: instead of 'the attacker ran a script', everyone writes T1059.001. For the attack chain itself, see the Endpoint Security map.

modules.title: The Framework
modules.desc: ATT&CK stands for Adversarial Tactics, Techniques, and Common Knowledge. It is a matrix: columns are tactics, cells are the techniques used to achieve them.

children.title: Built from observation
children.desc: Every technique is documented with real-world examples from incident reports, not theory. That is what makes it credible.

children.title: Matrices
children.desc: Enterprise (Windows, Linux, macOS, cloud, network, containers), Mobile, and ICS for industrial systems. SOC work is almost all Enterprise.

children.title: Common language
children.desc: An EDR detection, a threat report, and a SIEM rule can all point to the same technique ID, so they can be correlated.

children.title: Coverage mapping
children.desc: Mark which techniques your rules detect to see the gaps. ATT&CK Navigator is the free tool for colouring the matrix.

children.title: Threat-informed defense
children.desc: Look up which techniques the groups targeting your sector use, then check whether you detect those first.

children.title: Not a checklist
children.desc: Detecting every technique is neither possible nor the goal; some are normal admin behavior. Prioritize by threat and impact.

modules.title: Tactic vs Technique
modules.desc: The tactic is the attacker's goal at that step — the why. The technique is the method used to reach it — the how. One technique can serve several tactics.

children.title: Tactic
children.desc: A column such as Persistence (TA0003): 'I want to survive a reboot.' Enterprise has 14 tactics.

children.title: Technique
children.desc: A cell such as Scheduled Task/Job (T1053): one way to achieve persistence.

children.title: Sub-technique
children.desc: A more specific variant, written with a dot: T1053.005 Scheduled Task on Windows; T1059.001 PowerShell under Command and Scripting Interpreter.

children.title: Procedure
children.desc: The exact implementation a specific group or tool used — the concrete command line. Shown as examples on each technique page.

children.title: One technique, many tactics
children.desc: Valid Accounts (T1078) appears under Initial Access, Persistence, Privilege Escalation, and Defense Evasion, because stolen credentials serve all four goals.

children.title: ID prefixes
children.desc: TA tactic, T technique, M mitigation, G group, S software, DS data source, C campaign.

modules.title: Tactics 1–7
modules.desc: The first half of the Enterprise matrix, in the order an intrusion usually unfolds. Real attacks skip and repeat steps.

children.title: Reconnaissance
children.desc: TA0043 — gather information on the target: employees, exposed services, technologies.

children.title: Resource Development
children.desc: TA0042 — buy domains, rent servers, build or acquire malware, steal accounts.

children.title: Initial Access
children.desc: TA0001 — first foothold: phishing, exploiting a public-facing app, valid credentials.

children.title: Execution
children.desc: TA0002 — run attacker code: PowerShell, scripts, a user opening a file.

children.title: Persistence
children.desc: TA0003 — survive reboots and password changes: scheduled tasks, Run keys, new services or accounts.

children.title: Privilege Escalation
children.desc: TA0004 — gain higher rights: local exploits, misconfigurations, UAC bypass.

children.title: Defense Evasion
children.desc: TA0005 — avoid detection: disable security tools, inject into trusted processes, clear logs.

modules.title: Tactics 8–14
modules.desc: The second half: expanding through the network and achieving the goal.

children.title: Credential Access
children.desc: TA0006 — steal passwords and hashes: LSASS dumping, keylogging, brute force.

children.title: Discovery
children.desc: TA0007 — learn the environment: list users, domain admins, shares, other hosts.

children.title: Lateral Movement
children.desc: TA0008 — move to other systems: RDP, SMB with stolen hashes, remote services.

children.title: Collection
children.desc: TA0009 — gather the data of interest: files, email, screenshots, clipboard.

children.title: Command and Control
children.desc: TA0011 — talk to attacker infrastructure: HTTPS beacons, DNS tunneling.

children.title: Exfiltration
children.desc: TA0010 — get data out: over the C2 channel, to cloud storage.

children.title: Impact
children.desc: TA0040 — the final damage: encryption for ransom, data destruction, service disruption.

modules.title: Linked Objects
modules.desc: Each technique page connects to other object types. Following those links answers the defender's questions about a technique.

children.title: Detection
children.desc: How to notice the technique in telemetry — what to watch and which behavior is suspicious. Newer ATT&CK versions organize this as detection strategies and analytics.

children.title: Mitigation
children.desc: Controls that prevent the technique or reduce its effect, with M IDs: M1032 Multi-factor Authentication, M1026 Privileged Account Management, M1038 Execution Prevention.

children.title: Data Sources
children.desc: Which logs you need to see the technique at all, split into data components: Process (process creation), Command (command execution), Network Traffic (flow). No data source, no detection.

children.title: Software / Malware
children.desc: Named tools and malware with S IDs. 'Malware' is attacker-built (Emotet); 'tool' is legitimate software abused (Mimikatz S0002, PsExec, Cobalt Strike S0154).

children.title: Groups
children.desc: Tracked threat actors with G IDs, each listing the techniques and software they are known to use.

children.title: Campaigns
children.desc: A set of intrusions over a period with shared goals, given C IDs — for example the SolarWinds compromise.

modules.title: APT
modules.desc: A well-resourced, usually state-linked group that targets specific organizations and stays inside for a long time. The word describes the attacker, not the malware.

children.title: Advanced
children.desc: Custom tooling and zero-days when needed — though many APTs happily use phishing and public tools when those work.

children.title: Persistent
children.desc: A long-term objective rather than a quick payout; dwell time can be months, and they return after being evicted.

children.title: Motivation
children.desc: Espionage, sabotage, or for some states, revenue. Financially driven crime groups are often tracked the same way (FIN groups).

children.title: Names differ by vendor
children.desc: The same group has many names: APT29 is Cozy Bear (CrowdStrike) and Midnight Blizzard (Microsoft). ATT&CK lists the aliases on each group page.

children.title: Why a SOC cares
children.desc: Knowing which groups target your sector and region tells you which techniques to prioritize and which IOCs to hunt for.

modules.title: APT Examples
modules.desc: Well-documented groups and a known operation of each. Attribution comes from governments and vendors; it is rarely certain.

children.title: APT28 · G0007
children.desc: Fancy Bear, attributed to Russia's GRU. Breach of the US Democratic National Committee (2016), German Bundestag (2015).

children.title: APT29 · G0016
children.desc: Cozy Bear / Midnight Blizzard, attributed to Russia's SVR. The SolarWinds supply-chain compromise (2020), in which a poisoned software update reached around 18,000 customers.

children.title: Lazarus Group · G0032
children.desc: Attributed to North Korea, financially motivated. Sony Pictures (2014), the $81M Bangladesh Bank SWIFT theft (2016), WannaCry (2017), and the roughly $1.5B Bybit crypto theft (2025).

children.title: Sandworm · G0034
children.desc: Attributed to Russia's GRU. Ukrainian power grid outages (2015, 2016) and NotPetya (2017), destructive malware disguised as ransomware.

children.title: APT41 · G0096
children.desc: Attributed to China. Unusual mix of state espionage and personal financial crime, including supply-chain attacks and video game industry intrusions.

children.title: Carbanak · G0008
children.desc: Financially motivated group that compromised banks' internal networks and moved money via ATMs and transfers from around 2013. Relevant to any banking SOC.
